stem:
A 41-year-old woman with biopsy-proven pulmonary sarcoidosis has two weeks of thirst, constipation and passing large volumes of urine. She takes no supplements. Her adjusted serum calcium is raised and her parathyroid hormone level is suppressed.

Which mechanism best explains the raised calcium?

options.A: Autonomous parathyroid hormone secretion from a single enlarged parathyroid adenoma
options.B: Osteolytic bone destruction by widespread metastatic deposits within the skeleton
options.C: Reduced renal calcium excretion because of chronic granulomatous kidney scarring
options.D: Increased bone resorption driven by a persistently high circulating parathyroid hormone level
options.E: Activation of vitamin D by granuloma macrophages, independent of parathyroid hormone

correct_answer: E. Activation of vitamin D by granuloma macrophages, independent of parathyroid hormone
why_correct: Macrophages in sarcoid granulomas express 1-alpha-hydroxylase and convert 25-hydroxyvitamin D to calcitriol without the normal feedback control. The excess calcitriol increases intestinal calcium absorption and bone resorption, so calcium rises and parathyroid hormone is suppressed. This is why a low or low-normal parathyroid hormone in a patient with granulomatous disease points away from a parathyroid cause. Source: standard teaching on granulomatous hypercalcaemia (sarcoidosis).
why_wrong: A. A parathyroid adenoma would give a raised or inappropriately normal parathyroid hormone, not a suppressed one. B. Bone metastases can cause hypercalcaemia, but nothing here suggests malignancy and it would not explain the link with sarcoidosis. C. Granulomatous kidney scarring is not the usual mechanism; extrarenal calcitriol production is. D. A high parathyroid hormone level contradicts the suppressed result given in the stem.
pearl: In sarcoidosis the hypercalcaemia is parathyroid hormone independent, so a suppressed parathyroid hormone with raised calcium should make you think of calcitriol-producing granulomas (or malignancy), and vitamin D supplements can worsen it.
thinking: Sarcoidosis with symptomatic hypercalcaemia  ↓  Parathyroid hormone is suppressed, so the parathyroid glands are not the cause  ↓  Granuloma macrophages hydroxylate vitamin D without feedback  ↓  Excess calcitriol raises gut absorption and bone resorption  ↓  Vitamin D activation by granuloma macrophages
exam_trap: A, a parathyroid adenoma, is the commonest cause of hypercalcaemia overall, but the suppressed parathyroid hormone in this stem rules it out.
takeaway: Hypercalcaemia with a suppressed parathyroid hormone in sarcoidosis comes from macrophage production of active vitamin D.
notes: Rewritten as a clinical vignette with PTH suppressed given in the stem (angle: PTH-independent calcitriol mechanism; same key as source). Source key and explanations checked as sound standard teaching. No live PLAB 1 item tests the sarcoid calcitriol mechanism (searched sarcoid/calcium/calcitriol/1-alpha-hydroxylase; RES025 is sarcoid diagnosis only, END/CR items are primary hyperparathyroidism or malignancy). CKS not fetched.

stem:
A 66-year-old man with severe COPD attends a stable outpatient review. His arterial blood gas shows a raised carbon dioxide tension and a bicarbonate above the reference range, with a pH close to normal.

Which renal adaptation, developing over several days, accounts for the raised bicarbonate?

options.A: Increased urinary excretion of bicarbonate to counter the acidosis over several days
options.B: Greater tubular bicarbonate reabsorption with extra acid excreted as ammonium
options.C: Reduced glomerular filtration to conserve the circulating buffer in the blood stream
options.D: Suppressed ammonium production by the proximal tubular cells of the nephron
options.E: Decreased hydrogen-ion secretion by the cells lining the collecting duct

correct_answer: B. Greater tubular bicarbonate reabsorption with extra acid excreted as ammonium
why_correct: Chronic carbon dioxide retention lowers blood pH, and over several days the kidneys compensate by reabsorbing more filtered bicarbonate and generating new bicarbonate while excreting extra hydrogen ions, largely as ammonium. This raises plasma bicarbonate and brings the pH back towards normal, which is the pattern of compensated chronic type 2 respiratory failure. Source: standard teaching on renal compensation in respiratory acidosis.
why_wrong: A. Excreting bicarbonate would worsen the acidosis rather than compensate for it. C. A fall in filtration is not the compensatory mechanism and would not raise bicarbonate. D. Ammonium production rises, not falls, to excrete the acid load. E. Hydrogen-ion secretion increases in this setting, so a decrease would be the wrong direction.
pearl: A high bicarbonate with a near-normal pH in a patient with a high carbon dioxide implies chronic retention with renal compensation, whereas a low pH implies the compensation has been overwhelmed or the rise is acute.
thinking: Chronic COPD with raised carbon dioxide  ↓  Respiratory acidosis lowers pH  ↓  Kidneys respond over days, not minutes  ↓  They retain bicarbonate and excrete more acid  ↓  Increased bicarbonate reabsorption with more hydrogen-ion excretion
exam_trap: A, increased bicarbonate excretion, is tempting if the direction of compensation is muddled, but losing bicarbonate would deepen the acidosis.
takeaway: Chronic carbon dioxide retention is compensated by renal bicarbonate retention and acid excretion over days.
notes: Re-angled as a stable outpatient gas needing the renal mechanism (source was a bare one-line recall). Key unchanged. Distinct from CR001 (acute-on-chronic gas interpretation, tests diagnosis not mechanism) and PAAKT016. Standard teaching, no URL fetched.
Duplicate: acute severe asthma initial treatment already live as RES006, BX934, BX388, PAQ12694 and BX590.
Duplicate: sudden breathlessness with pleuritic pain suggesting PE already live as BX144, BX550, PAQ15448, S058 and OG059.
Duplicate: grading acute severe asthma (cannot complete sentences, PEF 33-50%) already live as RES029 and RES006.
Duplicate: alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency with emphysema and liver disease already live as BX846, BX133, RES043, PAN3452 and PAN4503.

stem:
A 72-year-old woman with COPD attends pulmonary rehabilitation because she becomes breathless on stairs and panics when it starts. The physiotherapist teaches her to breathe in gently through her nose and then out slowly through pursed lips, as if cooling hot soup.

What is the main physiological benefit of this technique?

options.A: It increases inspiratory flow so that a larger tidal volume is drawn in
options.B: It raises carbon dioxide levels to stimulate a stronger respiratory drive
options.C: It strengthens the diaphragm by adding resistance to every inspiration
options.D: It slows expiration and holds small airways open, reducing air trapping
options.E: It generates a rapid expiratory flow that helps to clear the sputum

correct_answer: D. It slows expiration and holds small airways open, reducing air trapping
why_correct: Breathing out slowly against pursed lips creates a small back-pressure that splints the narrowed small airways open during expiration. This reduces dynamic air trapping and hyperinflation, lowers respiratory rate and helps the patient regain control of breathlessness. It is a standard breathing-control technique taught in COPD self-management and pulmonary rehabilitation. Source: standard teaching in COPD self-management (pulmonary rehabilitation is recommended in NICE NG115).
why_wrong: A. The technique slows breathing and does not aim to increase inspiratory flow. B. It does not deliberately raise carbon dioxide and could not safely be used for that purpose. C. Resistance to inspiration describes inspiratory muscle training, which is a different intervention. E. Rapid forced expiration is the active cycle of breathing or huff technique used for secretions, not pursed-lip breathing.
pearl: Pursed-lip breathing is gentle and slow, with a longer expiration than inspiration; forced rapid exhalation is a different technique used for sputum clearance.
thinking: COPD with exertional breathlessness and panic  ↓  Breath out slowly through pursed lips  ↓  Back-pressure holds the small airways open  ↓  Less air trapping and a slower breathing rate  ↓  Slowed expiration with reduced air trapping
exam_trap: E, rapid expiratory flow to clear sputum, confuses pursed-lip breathing with huffing, which is a forced technique for secretions.
takeaway: Pursed-lip breathing keeps small airways open during slow expiration and reduces air trapping in COPD.
notes: Source asked only for the technique name; the vignette describes the technique and the question asks its mechanism (same learning point: pursed-lip breathing in COPD). No live item mentions pursed-lip breathing (searched). NG115 fetched but contains no pursed-lip recommendation, so the source line cites standard teaching.

stem:
A 61-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with sudden breathlessness and pleuritic chest pain. She takes oestrogen-containing hormone therapy and has an oxygen saturation of 94% on air. She had a deep vein thrombosis in her left leg two years ago. The clinician starts to apply the two-level Wells score for pulmonary embolism.

Which of her features contributes to that score?

options.A: A previous episode of deep vein thrombosis
options.C: Her current use of oestrogen-containing hormone therapy
options.D: The pleuritic quality of her chest pain
options.E: Her oxygen saturation below 95% on air

correct_answer: A. A previous episode of deep vein thrombosis
why_correct: The two-level PE Wells score includes clinical signs of DVT, PE being the most likely diagnosis, a heart rate above 100 beats per minute, recent immobilisation or surgery, a previous DVT or PE, haemoptysis and active cancer. A previous DVT therefore scores, and the total decides whether a CTPA or a D-dimer comes next. Source: NICE NG158, venous thromboembolic diseases, recommendation 1.1.17.
why_wrong: B. Age over 50 is part of the PERC rule used to rule out PE in low-risk patients and is not a Wells item. C. Oestrogen use features in the PERC rule but does not score in the Wells PE score. D. The pleuritic quality of the pain is common in PE but is not scored. E. Saturation below 95% is a PERC criterion, not a Wells criterion.
pearl: Wells PE and PERC overlap (previous VTE, haemoptysis, heart rate) but age, oestrogen use and low saturation belong only to PERC.
thinking: Suspected PE  ↓  Wells score estimates clinical probability  ↓  Score items: DVT signs, PE most likely, heart rate, immobility or surgery, previous VTE, haemoptysis, cancer  ↓  Age, oestrogen and saturation are PERC items  ↓  Previous DVT
exam_trap: C, oestrogen therapy, is a recognised VTE risk factor and is in PERC, so it tempts, but it does not score in the Wells PE tool.
takeaway: Previous DVT or PE scores in the Wells PE tool, whereas age, oestrogen use and low saturation belong to PERC.
notes: Changed angle from bare list recall to applying the score to a patient whose listed features include scoring and non-scoring items; key is a previous DVT (no threshold). Source AKT key was verified against NG158 table 2 (recommendation 1.1.17). Existing live items (CR024, CR044, ACU020, BX549) test next steps after the score, not its components. NG158 fetched.
Same learning point as my own PAN3954 (stony dullness = effusion); BX266 also live. Not repeated within batch.
Duplicate: asthma unable to complete sentences means acute severe asthma already live as BX590, BX388, RES006, RES029 and PAN447.
Duplicate: silent chest as a life-threatening asthma feature already live in RES001, RES029 and PAQ16091.
Duplicate/low-value: falling peak flow signalling worsening asthma already live in PAN447, RES029, PAQ225 and CR033.
Duplicate: severe asthma, cannot complete sentences, treat urgently already live as RES006, RES029, BX388, BX934 and BX590.
Duplicate: controlled oxygen in COPD at risk of hypercapnia already live as RES030, BX933, PAN1748 and PAQ15182.
Duplicate: life-threatening asthma features (exhaustion, low saturation, poor air entry) already live as PAQ16091, RES001 and RES029.

stem:
A 68-year-old retired man spent thirty years working at an underground coal face. He now has several years of gradually worsening exertional breathlessness and a chronic cough. A chest radiograph shows multiple small nodular opacities, most marked in the upper zones, and there is no pleural thickening.

Which occupational lung disease is most likely?

options.A: Coal workers' pneumoconiosis from long-term inhaled mine dust
options.B: Malignant mesothelioma arising after earlier asbestos exposure
options.C: Byssinosis due to repeated exposure to raw cotton dust
options.D: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis from inhaled mouldy hay spores
options.E: Occupational asthma caused by sensitisation to isocyanates

correct_answer: A. Coal workers' pneumoconiosis from long-term inhaled mine dust
why_correct: Prolonged inhalation of coal dust causes coal workers' pneumoconiosis, with small nodular opacities, typically in the upper zones, and slowly progressive breathlessness and cough. A detailed occupational history is the key to recognising it. Source: standard teaching on occupational lung disease (pneumoconiosis).
why_wrong: B. Mesothelioma follows asbestos exposure and presents with pleural thickening, effusion or a pleural mass rather than diffuse upper-zone nodules. C. Byssinosis occurs in cotton and textile workers. D. Hypersensitivity pneumonitis is linked to organic dusts such as mouldy hay and is not related to coal. E. Isocyanate asthma causes variable airflow obstruction with a normal or non-specific radiograph.
pearl: Always take a lifetime occupational history in breathlessness; the dust determines the disease, so match the job to the pattern on the radiograph.
thinking: Long exposure at a coal face  ↓  Progressive breathlessness and cough  ↓  Nodular opacities in the upper zones without pleural disease  ↓  Coal dust is the cause  ↓  Coal workers' pneumoconiosis
exam_trap: B, mesothelioma, is the best-known occupational lung disease, but it is caused by asbestos and shows pleural disease, not nodular opacities.
takeaway: A coal miner with progressive breathlessness and nodular upper-zone opacities has coal workers' pneumoconiosis.
notes: New vignette with the radiographic pattern given; key unchanged and sound. No live item covers coal workers' pneumoconiosis (DT120 is silicosis with TB; RES024 and PAQ15445 are asbestos). Option distractor set re-worded. Standard teaching, no URL fetched.

stem:
A 71-year-old man who smoked heavily for fifty years has progressive breathlessness on exertion. He has a barrel-shaped chest, hyperresonant percussion and quiet breath sounds. CT shows enlarged airspaces and lung function testing shows a very low gas transfer. A pathologist later examines tissue from a lung resection.

Which pathological change is characteristic of his condition?

options.A: Permanent dilatation of the bronchi with chronic bacterial infection
options.B: Interstitial fibrosis that thickens the walls of the alveoli
options.C: Destruction of alveolar walls with loss of elastic recoil
options.D: Hypertrophy of mucous glands with excess goblet cells
options.E: Eosinophilic airway inflammation with reversible smooth-muscle contraction

correct_answer: C. Destruction of alveolar walls with loss of elastic recoil
why_correct: Emphysema is defined by destruction of the walls of the airspaces distal to the terminal bronchioles. Loss of alveolar tissue and elastic recoil causes air trapping and hyperinflation, and the loss of surface area for gas exchange explains the very low gas transfer. Source: standard teaching on COPD pathology.
why_wrong: A. Permanent bronchial dilatation defines bronchiectasis. B. Interstitial fibrosis causes restrictive disease with a reduced lung volume, not hyperinflation. D. Mucous gland hypertrophy is the feature of chronic bronchitis. E. Eosinophilic inflammation with reversible bronchoconstriction describes asthma.
pearl: Emphysema is a pathological diagnosis (alveolar destruction), whereas chronic bronchitis is a clinical one (chronic productive cough); both sit within COPD.
thinking: Heavy smoker with hyperinflation and low gas transfer  ↓  Hyperresonant, barrel chest  ↓  Alveolar walls are lost  ↓  Elastic recoil falls and air is trapped  ↓  Destruction of alveolar walls
exam_trap: D, mucous gland hypertrophy, is also a smoking-related COPD change, but it defines chronic bronchitis, not the loss of alveolar tissue.
takeaway: Emphysema is destruction of alveolar walls with air trapping and a low gas transfer.
notes: New vignette (CT and gas transfer wording, pathology question). Key unchanged. No live item tests emphysema pathology (RES043, BX133 and the alpha-1 antitrypsin items test aetiology). Standard teaching, no URL fetched.

stem:
A 63-year-old woman who was treated for breast cancer some years ago has had three weeks of increasing breathlessness. On the right, chest expansion is reduced, the percussion note at the base is stony dull, and both breath sounds and vocal resonance are diminished. The trachea is central.

What is the most likely cause of these findings?
why_correct: Fluid in the pleural space gives a stony dull percussion note with reduced expansion, breath sounds and vocal resonance over the effusion. In a woman with previous breast cancer a malignant effusion is a leading consideration, and a chest radiograph or ultrasound confirms it. Source: standard teaching on respiratory examination (pleural effusion).
why_wrong: A. Consolidation gives dullness with bronchial breathing and increased vocal resonance. C. Pneumothorax gives a hyperresonant note. D. Lobar collapse usually draws the trachea towards the affected side and gives bronchial rather than simply diminished breath sounds. E. Pulmonary fibrosis causes bilateral fine inspiratory crackles with a normal percussion note.
pearl: Dull with reduced breath sounds and vocal resonance is fluid; dull with bronchial breathing and increased resonance is consolidation.
thinking: Breathlessness with unilateral basal signs  ↓  Stony dull percussion  ↓  Reduced breath sounds and vocal resonance  ↓  Fluid rather than solid lung  ↓  Pleural effusion
exam_trap: A, consolidation, also causes basal dullness, but it brings bronchial breathing and increased vocal resonance rather than reduced sounds.
takeaway: Stony dullness with reduced breath sounds and vocal resonance means pleural effusion.
notes: New vignette (breast cancer history, vocal resonance and trachea given). BX266 (heart failure, bilateral dullness, key effusions) is the nearest live item: same sign pattern, but different patient, unilateral, and discriminates from consolidation and collapse; flagged for checker. Standard teaching, no URL fetched.
Duplicate: early-onset basal emphysema in a non-smoker as alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency already live as RES043, PAN4503, BX133 and BX846.
Duplicate: chronic lung disease with right heart failure (cor pulmonale/pulmonary hypertension) already live as PAN2158, PAN8280 and CARD063.
